title: Nickel exposure at CATL plant in Hungary - electrive.com
content:
The occupational safety authority in CATL's battery plant in Debrecen, Hungary, has temporarily suspended work in three areas when nine employees were found to have experienced elevated nickel exposure. The incident affects CATL amid the already delayed ramp-up of its cell production.
Module production (pictured) has already begun at CATL in Debrecen, but cell manufacturing has not yet started.
Image: CATL
Authorities stopped work in some areas of CATL’s plant in Debrecen, Hungary, after CATL reported that nine employees had been exposed to elevated levels of nickel. A subsequent occupational safety inspection by authorities in Hajdú-Bihar County found that workers had not been adequately provided with protective equipment.
According to Hungarian media, local authorities have prohibited work in three areas of the cell manufacturing building until the identified deficiencies are rectified. The affected areas include systems for laser cutting cathode and anode foils, winding electrode foils, and cell drying. Reports also indicate that a procedure to impose a fine is underway.
However, the suspension of work does not amount to a complete production stop at the site. While cell manufacturing in Debrecen has not yet commenced as the plant is still being developed, CATL is already producing battery modules. In May, the Chinese battery manufacturer commissioned a new
module assembly line with an annual capacity of 5 GWh
on its premises. The cells required for this continue to be sourced from other CATL plants.
CATL awaits full approval for cell production
Alongside the occupational safety measures, approvals for cell production have also hit some hurdles. The two processes are separate. The authority denied the usage permit for the second expansion stage not because of nickel exposure, but due to a deficiency in formal proceedings. A permit was initially rejected on 19 August when a completed building was not correctly represented in a site plan. However, during the first expansion stage, the authority granted the usage permit on 25 August after missing documents were submitted.
The incident comes at a challenging time for CATL as it ramps up production. The cell factory was initially designed for an annual capacity of 40 GWh. While the company says the plant has been completed, cell production is behind schedule. As the end of last year, CATL had projected the start of
series production for March or April 2026
The delays have already impacted Mercedes-Benz. The batteries for the new electric van VLE were originally supposed to come from Debrecen but are now being supplied from China. CATL is covering the additional costs incurred. BMW has not been affected so far, as the car manufacturer is not due to receive cells from the nearby CATL plant until
For CATL, the priority now is to resolve both the outstanding approval issues and the identified occupational safety deficiencies. It remains unclear whether the work ban in the three affected areas will further delay the start of cell production. In the long term, CATL plans to expand the production capacity in Debrecen to up to 100 GWh per year.

title: US declares ‘national emergency’ amid fears of cyber attacks on BESS, power sector – Batteries International
content: The US has declared a cyber security national emergency in a bid to protect battery energy storage systems and the wider power infrastructure from Trojan horse-style attacks. BESS and UPS systems are specifically included in an extensive list of potential cyber warfare targets among bulk-power system electrical equipment (BPSEE) produced abroad — which the US fears are at heightened risk. The energy systems cyber alert was outlined in an executive order signed by US president Donald Trump on August 26. The order — covered by the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the National Emergencies Act — largely prohibits certain foreign-made equipment from being bought or installed in the US, including critical software and digital capabilities. BPSEE covers a wide range of equipment and installations including power stations, backup power systems and grid-connected inverters. Trump said energy secretary Chris Wright will now work with cabinet colleagues and others to identify BPSEE that may pose risks and draw up a safeguards action list, with a particular focus on equipment linked to US-designated foreign entities of concern (FEOC). ‘Supply disruption’ “Since my first term, the threat to the US regarding foreign supply of bulk-power system electric equipment has become even more acute,” Trump said. “The rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, datacentres, artificial intelligence and defence production has increased the nation’s dependence on abundant, reliable electricity and magnified the consequences of a successful attack or supply disruption on the bulk-power system.” The president’s directive follows a report issued last month by the US Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), which warned as solar and energy storage continues to expand, cybersecurity protections become increasingly important to support grid reliability and resilience. SEIA cited a 2022 ransomware attack against the IT infrastructure of a wind turbine manufacturer in Germany, followed a year later by an attack that saw a third-party service provider lose remote data monitoring capabilities for around 2,000 turbines. ‘New risks loom’ Separately, in 2025, Poland successfully thwarted what officials described as the largest cyberattack on its energy infrastructure in years, SEIA said. Emerging technologies, including the deployment of advanced artificial intelligence models to optimise energy assets, create new cybersecurity risks and expand the attack surface. The association revealed it now runs a monthly cybersecurity working group dedicated to sharing latest cybersecurity policy, threat information and defence tactics for solar and energy storage systems. In the UK, the government confirmed that a power plant was shut down during a cyber attack in July 2026. Reliable media sources reported that the attack was carried out by hackers affiliated to the Iranian regime. The UK government declined to give details but said the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and National Cyber Security Centre have since warned power companies to be on their guard. EU cyber concerns A white paper published in December 2025, by global consulting firm the Brattle Group and US-based international operational technology cybersecurity specialists Dragos, said experts agreed that US infrastructure security concerns would likely lead to more stringent security measures towards FEOCs. In terms of the European Union, the white paper said the bloc’s Cyber Resilience Act, which goes into effect in 2027, will certify every product for sale in the EU meets European cybersecurity standards. However, while experts agreed that consistent, EU-wide policy was the correct method to approach grid cybersecurity, the white paper warned that member states without the same agenda or policies would create a lack of harmonisation among operators on the same grid. “Diverging rules between European countries create vulnerability to the highly interconnected European power network, resulting in higher regulatory compliance costs for investors and differing levels of cybersecurity implementation in the European internal energy market.” The white paper said BESS deployment over the next five years is expected to grow at 30% annually in the US, 45% in the EU and 20–25% across Japan, South Korea, Southeast Asia and India. “As BESS deployment accelerates, it is important that the increasing role of batteries in facilitating efficient clean energy and grid reliability is not undermined by cybersecurity vulnerabilities. “Conversely, BESS additions with strong cyber protection will contribute to lower levels of vulnerability for the grid as a whole.” Image credit: Envato The post US declares ‘national emergency’ amid fears of cyber attacks on BESS, power sector appeared first on Batteries International .

title: Schneider Electric home EV charger uses smart load management
content:
Charging
Automotive & Mobility
SmartAmp tech dynamically adjusts charging speed based on real-time household energy use to prevent overloads.
August 28, 2026
2 Min Read
Schneider Electric's new Schneider Charge residential EV charger features built-in SmartAmp technology that automatically adjusts charging speed based on real-time household energy use, helping homeowners add Level 2 charging with less complexity.
Schneider Electric
At a Glance
The charger delivers up to 11.5 kW AC power and includes OCPP 1.6 compliance for grid programs.
Installation is simplified with built-in load management, eliminating need for separate monitoring devices.
Schneider Electric Launches Home EV Charger
Electric component supplier Schneider is expanding beyond household plugs and
receptacles
EV chargers
with the announcement of
Schneider Charge
, an SAE Level 2 AC home EV charger.
Schneider Charge Pro
is the company’s existing commercial Level 2 EV charger for multi-unit dwellings, workplaces, fleets, and destination charging.
This new charger’s purpose is to simplify EV ownership for homeowners who aren’t interested in spending a lot of money upgrading their home’s electric service to meet the demands of EV charging. Sometimes electric service or the circuit breaker panel need to be upgraded to support a circuit for an EV charger, which can cost between $2,000 and $6,500.
The Schneider Charge EV charger is designed to work within the home’s existing electric capacity, avoiding the need for upgrades. Its SmartAmp technology is designed to automatically adjust charging speed based on real-time household energy use.
The UL 3141-compliant load management monitors household electrical use and adjusts the charger’s power level downward when appliances need power. It does this without separate monitoring devices or additional components.
When the home’s electrical supply can support it, the Schneider Charge system can deliver 11.5 kilowatts of AC power. It is OCPP 1.6 compliant to support future grid service programs too, but is not currently bi-directional.
"As homeowners buy EVs and add high-power electric technologies, many are realizing their existing electrical systems were not built for that level of demand," said Shawn Bonacorsi, Head of Electrification Solutions, Schneider Electric, North America Operations. "Schneider Charge helps remove that installation hurdle by enabling safe, reliable Level 2 charging within a home's existing electrical capacity, making EV charging simpler and easier at home, where most charging takes place."
There is even support for the installation process through home EV charger installer Omerit.
"For electricians and contractors, Schneider Charge is designed to make installation simpler and more efficient," Bonacorsi said. "By building load management into the charger, we're making home EV charging easier to install with less complexity and disruption for homeowners."
The Schneider Charge app lets homeowners monitor charging in real time, adjust settings, and schedule charging during lower-cost overnight hours.
Schneider Charge is available with either a traditional SAE J1772 plug or a Tesla-style North American Charging Standard (NACS) connector on its 25-foot cable that provides flexibility for reaching the EV’s charge port without hazardous extension cords. It will be available in both a hardwired version and a plug-in version, and hopefully Schneider will also provide EV-certified receptacles for the plug-in chargers, avoiding the
fires that are possible when using a range-grade 240-volt receptacle
for the continuous high load of an EV charger.

title: Cummins Wins Its Largest BESS Contract for US Data Center
content:
Stationary Batteries
Battery Manufacturing
Battery News
The 5MWh lithium iron phosphate system will manage AI-driven load fluctuations and help address community concerns about diesel generator noise and emissions.
August 27, 2026
3 Min Read
Cummins' LFP battery system
At a Glance
Cummins' largest BESS deployment will support AI-driven power fluctuations at a major U.S. data center facility
The 5MWh lithium iron phosphate system offers a quieter, cleaner alternative to diesel backup generators
Battery storage helps data centers overcome community opposition related to noise pollution and carbon emissions.
Cummins Inc. has secured a contract to supply battery energy storage systems (BESS) for a large U.S. data center project, marking the company's largest BESS deployment to date. The project underscores growing demand for energy storage solutions capable of managing AI-driven power fluctuations in hyperscale computing environments.
The BESS installation will support utility-defined requirements for managing load fluctuations associated with artificial intelligence workloads. The system is designed to rapidly charge or discharge to reduce demand spikes, improve power quality, and maintain stable load profiles at utility interconnection points. This capability helps mitigate the oscillating power demands characteristic of AI processing while enhancing ride-through performance during grid disturbances.
BESS as a path around community opposition
Data center projects increasingly face fierce community pushback over environmental concerns. According to a
Gallup survey
, 70% of Americans oppose data center construction in their area, with half of opponents citing excessive resource use and 16% mentioning pollution concerns including noise, air, and water pollution. Communities from
Chandler, Arizona to Greenbrier, Arkansas
have complained about constant humming from cooling systems and diesel generators, with residents reporting headaches, sleep disturbances, and hypertension from 24/7 noise.
Related:
7 Residential Battery Storage Systems Worth Buying in 2026
BESS technology is emerging as a solution that addresses many of these objections. Unlike diesel generators, battery storage systems operate with minimal noise—typically comparable to an HVAC unit—and produce zero on-site emissions during operation, eliminating the need for fuel storage and the associated pollution.
Studies show
that adding BESS can reduce a data center's overall carbon emissions by up to 60% when it displaces diesel usage. Major tech companies including Microsoft, Google, and Meta have initiated programs to replace diesel generators with BESS, with Microsoft committing to eliminate diesel by 2030. The lack of noise and emissions means
batteries can be deployed in urban or sensitive areas with far less community opposition
compared to diesel gensets.
However, BESS deployments face their own challenges.
Community concerns about fire safety and long-term environmental impacts
have emerged as deployment accelerates, making some projects harder to approve. Modern BESS designs address these concerns through advanced thermal management, fire suppression systems, and environmental safeguards built into the system architecture.
Related:
Understanding Base Power’s role in energy storage solutions
Cummins expands its power portfolio
The contract reflects Cummins' broader strategy to support data center infrastructure with diverse power solutions. According to Jenny Bush, president of Cummins' Power Systems business, the company now offers customers a range of options from diesel standby and natural gas prime power to BESS and integrated microgrid solutions.
"As demand for data center capacity continues to grow, Cummins is well positioned to support customers with a broad portfolio of power solutions," Bush said. "This project reinforces our commitment to helping customers build reliable, resilient and increasingly sustainable power infrastructure."
For data center developers facing grid constraints, lengthening interconnection queues, and rising energy costs, BESS is becoming a critical power enabler. The technology can accelerate deployment timelines, enhance resilience, and optimize available power capacity—particularly important as AI workloads drive unprecedented energy demands. Cummins' utility-scale BESS solution can be deployed as a bridge-to-grid solution, integrated with backup power systems, or incorporated into broader microgrid architectures. The flexibility allows customers to maximize available grid capacity, manage peak demand, and meet utility load-management requirements.
Related:
Advanced Testing Methods in Battery Manufacturing BESS Explained
Technical specifications
Cummins' BESS for data center applications features:
5MWh nominal capacity
Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery chemistry
Liquid cooling thermal management
Flexible DC block architecture compatible with multiple power conversion systems (PCS) and energy management systems (EMS)
Bridge-to-grid ready with integration capability for diesel and natural gas generators
Compliance with UL 9540A, UL 9540, UL 1973, NFPA 855, NFPA 68, IEEE 1547, and UL 1741 SA/SB standards
The system is designed specifically for hyperscale workloads and resilient operation in demanding data center environments. Cummins launched its BESS solutions in May 2025, backed by more than 100 years of power generation expertise.

This all followed more than a decade of teaching English, ESL, literature, and argumentation as a lecturer at Eastern Michigan University (Ypsilanti, MI) and, for five years, at Sakura no Seibo Junior College (Fukushima, Japan).

title: Trade and Tariffs: Inside the US-Canada Relationship Dispute
content:
Trade and Tariffs: Inside the US-Canada Relationship Dispute
Prioritise Us
on Google
Trade relationships between US and Canada face new levels of volatility | Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and US President Donald Trump. Credit: Wikimedia Commons
Following an attempt at a trade deal, the US and Canada's relationship is on unstable grounds, with threats and implementation of tariffs going both ways
Amid claims of an almost-achieved trade agreement, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has claimed that the proposed deal was uneven, with the US asking too much and giving too little back.
The deal was in place to reduce tariffs, which have shaken trade in recent years. Now, however, tensions have increased and trade between the two nations is at a volatile standing.
With counter offers and tariffs threats at a high, businesses across the US and Canada are left in a vulnerable position.
Preferential access to any major market is now a political variable, not a structural guarantee.
Scott Lehmann, GVP at Sphera
Trade disputes
Following months of back and forth upon US President Donald Trump's re-election, the trade relationship between the two nations may have reached a breaking point. Weeks of urgent talks came to a head, with results neither leader had desired.
Though Trump had briefly declared that the countries had reached a deal, Carney recalled negotiations on August 22, citing unfair trade agreements. According to Ottawa, the US attempted to make last-minute changes to the agreement, but the US disputes that and states the nation had attempted to turn away from earlier commitments.
The deal would have cut US tariffs on Canadian cars and light-duty trucks from 25% to 15%, and tariffs on steel and aluminium from 50% to 25%. In response, Canada was going to reduce tariffs on items and reduce import administration for dairy products.
Now, however, the countries are facing further disputes, with tariff threats at another high.
"The breakdown of
US-Canada trade
talks is the clearest example of how the world order that governed global trade for thirty years is ending," explains Scott Lehmann, Group Vice President at Sphera.
Scott Lehmann, Group Vice President at Sphera
"Trade has become power and the system is being rewired around leverage, resilience, industrial depth and strategic control. We have a front row seat to the unfolding of a harder, more selective, more political form of re-globalisation. The logic of great power competition, control resources, control markets, control supply chains, never quite disappeared; the vocabulary of globalisation and free trade simply obscured it for thirty years."
Policy and counter-offers
On July 20, the US invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 in order to implement
50% tariffs
on Canadian goods. Demands from Washington impacted Canadian trade policy autonomy and
critical mineral
access. In response, Canada has imposed counter-tariffs, which are effective from September 8.
These measures will mirror the US actions on a dollar-for-dollar basis, targeting more than 700 product categories from the US. This will include everyday consumer items such as toilet paper, clothing, seafood and cheese.
In a press conference, Canada’s Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne explained: “Canada's counter tariffs are designed primarily to provide protection for Canadian industry impacted by US tariffs and allow them to compete against US products in the Canadian market. It's all about fairness. It's all about level playing field. It's all about supporting Canadian workers and Canadian businesses."
François-Philippe Champagne, Finance Minister of Canada. Credit: Parliament of Canada
Canada exported approximately US$451bn worth of goods in 2025. Now, the US has
imposed tariffs
on Canadian exports such as hockey equipment, whiskey, textiles and auto parts, making up 4% of Canada's exports to the US.
These extra costs will be felt by the consumers and the companies – particularly the smaller business owners.
On the US side, Scott states that the impact will be mostly felt by parts suppliers and producers. He says, "Parts suppliers on the US side will absorb the worst of the cost.
Steel producers
have had over a year of Section 232 exposure to begin adjusting, and automakers have the balance sheets and lobbying operations to absorb short-term cost increases while pursuing exemptions. Parts suppliers have neither. They operate on thin margins, cannot pass costs upward to OEMs or downward to raw material suppliers without losing the contract, and a 50% stacked tariff likely eliminates their margins."
For these organisations, the impact may not be felt immediately. In Canada, however, the damage will be felt sooner and will be more widespread. Its export economy is reliant on the US, as ocean freight costs make trade to European and Asian buyers less cost-effective. Market diversification takes many years to securely put in place, meaning the market will see a major hit once these tariffs start taking place.
Unstable trade relationships
have been a constant in the last year, impacting job security, product cost and trade efficiency. This relationship breakdown is the newest in a long line, but the volatility may end before the new costs come to fruition.
"Preferential access to any major market is now a political variable, not a structural guarantee," Scott warns.
"The Canada situation will resolve. But not before it claims companies, jobs and supply chain relationships that took decades to build and cannot be reconstructed by the time the politics move on.”

title: Amex GBT: Exploring Supply Chain Impact on the Rental Market
content:
Amex GBT: Exploring Supply Chain Impact on the Rental Market
Prioritise Us
on Google
Amex GBT explores the state of the car rentals market amid ongoing geopolitical shifts. Credit: Unsplash
The car rental market is undergoing transformation, driven by geopolitical disruption, the growing demand of supply chain operations and electrification
American Express Global Business Travel (Amex GBT) has launched its Ground Monitor report, exploring how the
car rental market
is set to be transformed throughout 2026-27.
Various factors are contributing to a shift in the market, including the increasing uptake of electrification, as well as heightened logistics needs.
Amex GBT explores the current trends alongside global shifts, working to create more resilience within operations.
This recall activity is forcing operators to maintain larger fleets than necessary, adding operational costs that may translate to higher rental prices.
Joshua Collier, Global Business Consulting, Amex GBT
Influences on the market
The last few years have seen increasing instability and fluctuating prices across every market place. Though Amex GBT does anticipate car prices to grow somewhat throughout the next year, it estimates the prices will remain stable.
Factors driving these increases can be seen across the world, with geopolitical influences having disrupted trade significantly in recent years. Ongoing trade tensions, volatility in the Middle East, the
electrification transition
and global inflation are all impacting how operations run.
The four main influences of car prices are:
Supply and demand
- Amex GBT reports a better balance between supply and demand, which means car rental rates should be stable. As deliveries have been consistently keeping pace with demand around the world, there is a downward pressure on rental prices.
Geopolitical issues
- Though conflict in the Middle East rose prices immediately for air transport, the impact on auto supply chains is coming at a delay. Aluminium supply is being disrupted and car tires are increasing in price. As more cars become 'smart cars',
shortages
in semiconductor chips are a growing concern, caused – in part – due to reduced production of helium.
Smarter cars
- The increase in smart cars is making driver safer and more efficient, they are also more expensive. Fixing the vehicles requires specialist technicians, which increases the cost of service. According to Amex GBT, smarter cars increase the global recall list, which makes supply of them less reliable, translating into the need for rental providers to have larger inventory buffer.
Lower resale values
- For car rental companies, selling off cars acts as an important revenue stream. However, the used car sector across Europe and the US is seeing declining pricing for electric vehicles and internal combustion engine vehicles. This means less opportunity for used car sales, but also more upwards pressure on rental rates.
"The car rental industry has overcome supply shortages caused by semiconductor chip constraints," Joshua Collier, Global Business Consulting, Amex GBT says to Supply Chain Digital.
Joshua Collier, Global Business Consulting, Amex GBT
"While cost pressures from inflation, insurance, labour, maintenance and vehicle expenses persist, normalised fleet supply is expected to keep price increases modest."
Key facts
Amex GBT expects rates in the US to increase between 1.5% and 2%
In Brazil, EV growth in rental fleet in 2025 was up 124.5% from the year before
In France, Amex GBT forecasts a 0.5% rate increase
Regional shifts
The Amex GBT report explores regional differences regarding the rental market, looking at North America, Latin America, Europe and Asia-Pacific.
Following minimal GDP growth and improved supply rates, Amex GBT predicts modest increases to car rental rates across Canada and the US. A cause for concern surrounds city surcharges, which are becoming more common in the region.
In Latin America, the rental sector is undergoing a steady growth, due to an increase in demand regarding both leisure and corporate operations. EVs in particular are seeing a growth – in the space of four years, Brazil's rental fleet grew from 2,545 vehicles to 33,562.
Across Europe, Amex GBT is predicting a varied increase, with flat to moderate growth. In the Netherlands, a high rate is anticipated due to rising motor vehicle taxes. Fleet scarcity is resulting in modest rate rises in Germany, with lower rates in the UK due to strong competition.
Amex GBT expects Australia to see some of the largest rental rate increases. In remote mining locations, competition is limited which can translate to higher price increases.
Joshua adds: "As supply stabilises, we are monitoring a range of dynamics that could determine whether rates hold steady or rise in business travel. Used car market
volatility is weakening
– used car prices are forcing rental companies to adjust fleet book values downward, creating cost pressures that could push rates up. Another influence is manufacturer fleet recalls growing. This recall activity is forcing operators to maintain larger fleets than necessary, adding operational costs that may translate to higher rental prices."
Electric Vehicles are impacting cost for rental companies. Credit: Getty Images
Meeting demands
Amid the ongoing electrification transition, businesses are expected to
add more sustainability
into their fleets. This means more sustainable fuels and more EVs. However, this is a major cost to companies, especially those which are newer or smaller.
Though using sustainable fuel or EVs is more cost-efficient in the long-term, the initial cost of purchasing can be a major hit to companies. As a result, many supply chain businesses use rental companies to meet new regulations and standards.
Renting instead of purchasing allows for the quick integration of sustainable options at a significantly lower cost. This means they can meet consumer expectations and meet the guidelines from reporting standards.
This has had its own issues, of course, as business owners around the world move towards rentals. Auto supply chains have mostly recovered following various shocks in recent years, but volatility is something owners need to be aware of.
"When it comes to car rental companies, today they operate more as asset management companies, prioritising residual value optimisation and cost control over actual fleet size," Joshua explains.
"In turn, that ensures that car rental companies are in greater control of their fleets and are less reliant on the manufacturer than previously. Whilst there would be some short-term insulation in the event of vehicle shortages, ultimately access to fleet supply is the number one factor that influences prices in the car rental market."
Amex GBT also suggests that business owners should work with a single rental provider for
fleet management
and car rentals, as it helps drive cohesion and reliability. Moreover, there needs to be collaboration between colleagues across the organisation to ensure visibility across HR, procurement, operations, legal and finance.

title: Court Limits Pentagon Use of Supply Chain Risk Label
content:
Court Limits Pentagon Use of Supply Chain Risk Label
Prioritise Us
on Google
A US judge has ruled that Anthropic's supply chain risk designation be removed (Image source: Getty Images/Mariakray)
Judge Rita Lin ruled the Pentagon's supply chain risk designation against Anthropic unlawful, a first-of-its-kind use of the FASCSA tool
Anthropic a "supply chain risk" earlier this year, a designation that had, until now, been reserved almost exclusively for companies linked to foreign adversaries.
US District Judge Rita Lin, ruling on 27 August 2026 in the Northern District of California, ordered the designation removed. She added that the Department of Defense's actions “constituted unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment” and that Anthropic “was denied the pre-deprivation process required under the Fifth Amendment”.
The ruling matters beyond the specifics of one company's dispute with the Pentagon. It tests the boundaries of a legal tool that determines which vendors an entire chain of government contractors is permitted to work with.
What the supply chain risk label actually does
The designation stems from the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018 (FASCSA), which established the Federal Acquisition Security Council to assess
national security risk
in the federal technology supply chain and recommend exclusion or removal orders against specific vendors.
In the past, FASCSA orders have targeted companies with ties to nations designated as adversarial. The first public order issued under the Act, in September 2025, excluded
cybersecurity
firm Acronis AG and its affiliates from Intelligence Community contracts. Anthropic's case marks a significant departure: it is the first time the tool has been used against a US-founded company over a policy dispute rather than a foreign-ownership concern.
Key facts: the Pentagon-Anthropic dispute
The Department of Defense sought to use Anthropic's Claude model for “all lawful purposes”, including sensitive military and intelligence applications.
Anthropic maintained guardrails preventing its models being used in fully autonomous lethal weapons or mass surveillance of Americans.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth designated Anthropic a supply chain risk in February 2026, barring the Pentagon and its contractors from using its products.
Anthropic filed suit in March 2026, arguing the designation was retaliation for its public position on AI safety.
A second, related lawsuit brought by Anthropic remains before a Washington, DC court.
Why the judge ruled against the Pentagon
Judge Lin found the government's stated justification did not hold up to scrutiny, ruling that the measures imposed on Anthropic were “illegal and baseless”. She noted that the Pentagon continued pursuing work with Anthropic even after issuing the designation, undermining its own claim of distrust.
“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics.”
Judge Rita Lin, US District Judge, Northern District of California
Announcing the original designation in February, Hegseth said “America's warfighters will never be held hostage by the ideological whims of Big Tech”, framing the move as a defence of military autonomy over vendor choice. The Department of Justice is expected to challenge the ruling.
An Anthropic spokesperson welcomed the decision, saying the company remains focused on working with the government to ensure the
benefits of AI reach
“so all Americans”.
Anthropic welcomed the decision, saying it remains focused on working with the government. Credit: Anthropic
Why this matters beyond one company
For federal contractors and their suppliers, a
supply chain risk designation
is not a minor procurement flag. It can bar an entire tier of contractors, not just the named company, from using a vendor's products. As a result, it is one of the most consequential tools available to federal agencies for reshaping a supply chain overnight.
The ruling does not challenge the Pentagon's right to choose its vendors freely, something Judge Lin explicitly affirmed. What it curtails is the use of a national security mechanism as leverage in a commercial or policy disagreement, a distinction that matters to any technology vendor operating inside federal supply chains, particularly as AI procurement across defence and intelligence agencies continues to expand.
Key company in focus: Anthropic
Anthropic is an AI safety and research company headquartered in San Francisco, California, and the developer of the Claude family of AI models. Dario Amodei serves as Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer. The company has publicly maintained safety guardrails restricting its models from use in autonomous weapons systems and mass surveillance applications.

title: Volkswagen unveils the first California EV camper, and it's based on the ID. Buzz [Images]
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 28 2026 - 8:07 am PT
The ID. California Cruise is
Volkswagen’s
first fully electric California camper. Based on the ID. Buzz, the camper van comes with a bed, window blinds, and other camping gear.
Volkswagen reveals the ID. California Cruise EV camper
It’s real! Volkswagen is finally giving the people what they want — a fully electric, zero-emission camper van.
The ID. California Cruise debuted at Caravan Salon 2026 as Volkswagen’s first all-electric California. It will be the first of a new family of California EVs that VW plans to introduce over the next few years.
Since the ID. Buzz went on sale in 2022, drivers, media, and camping enthusiasts have “repeatedly expressed interest in a California version of the all-electric Bulli,” Volkswagen said.
The ID. California Cruise is Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles’ “first concrete response,” with the first customer deliveries scheduled for early 2027.
Designed for weekend getaways, camping, and longer road trips, the ID. California Cruise comes with everything needed for an overnight (or a few) stay.
Inside, it offers enough sleeping space for two with a bed that’s 2.03 meters (6.66 ft) long and 1.20 meters (3.93 ft) wide.
Volkswagen ID. California Cruise EV camper bed setup (Source: VW Commercial Vehicles)
The EV camper van also features a newly developed 9 cm thick folding comfort mattress, ventilation grilles on the front side windows, and blackout blinds on all windows.
As an added bonus, Volkswagen is throwing in two camping chairs and a table. The optional panoramic glass roof also includes a matching blackout blind.
Volkswagen ID. California Cruise EV camper interior (Source: VW Commercial Vehicles)
Volkswagen Commercial Vehicles teamed up with Stuff Bubble, known for the world’s first inflatable camping kitchen,
to develop equipment
that turns an everyday van into a “fully-fledged camper in just a few minutes.” All components can easily be stored in the vehicle.
The interior features exclusive seat covers with integrated California woodwork, plus California lettering at the rear and special “Cruise” badges along the side.
Volkswagen ID. California Cruise EV camper is based on the ID. Buzz (Source: VW Commercial Vehicles)
Based on the ID. Buzz Pro, the electric California will be available with short or long wheelbases. It comes with added standard equipment, including the Interior Style Package, Comfort Package, and PowerSocket discharge adapter for vehicle-to-load (V2L) functions.
With V2L capabilities, the camper van becomes a mobile power source with a continuous output of up to 2,000 watts and a peak output of 3.6 kW. It can power a coffee pot, laptop, kitchen equipment, and other external devices, or charge an e-bike or e-scooter.
Volkswagen ID. California Cruise EV camper can power external electronic devices with V2L (Source: VW Commercial Vehicles)
Another cool feature is the California mode. Developed specifically for camping, it enables selected lights, USB ports, and comfort functions to run overnight, or up to 48 hours, Volkswagen said.
To top it off, VW Commercial Vehicles is introducing new “electric-trip” functions to the California App. For the first time, drivers can now find and navigate to charging stops along their trip. With Plug & Charge, charging sessions start automatically without the need for a physical payment method.
Volkswagen has yet to reveal all the details, but since it’s based on the ID. Buzz Pro, we have a good idea of what to expect.
The ID. Buzz SWB uses a 79 kWh battery with a WLTP range of up to 461 km (286 miles). The LWB version, on the other hand, uses an 86 kWh battery that delivers up to 487 km (302 miles) of range. Keep in mind, the camping equipment will likely impact range to some extent.
Prices for the ID. California Cruise start at €60,761
in Germany
, or about $70,500. The first customer deliveries are set to begin in early 2027.
Electrek’s Take
Will VW bring the electric California camper van to the US? Don’t get your hopes up. Volkswagen doesn’t currently sell the California in the US, so the electric version isn’t expected to make the trip overseas either.
Volkswagen did, however, introduce a new Tourer model for
the 2027 ID. Buzz
lineup that essentially converts it into a camper van with a fold-out bed, Overnight mode, and blackout shades.

the Kia PV5
(which, sadly, isn’t sold in the US)? Drop your pick in the comments below.

title: BYD Q2 profit jumps 30% as record exports offset weak China sales
content:
Fred Lambert
| Aug 28 2026 - 7:52 am PT
BYD posted its first quarterly profit increase in more than a year, with second-quarter net profit rising 29.8% to 8.2 billion yuan ($1.22 billion) as a record surge in exports offset a weak Chinese market.
The rebound ends four straight quarters of profit declines and reverses the 55.4% collapse BYD reported just three months earlier.
The quarter turned, but the first half is still down
Despite the Q2 recovery, BYD’s first-half results remain lower year-over-year. Revenue for the six months through June fell 7.13% to 344.82 billion yuan ($50.9 billion), and net profit attributable to shareholders dropped 20.54% to 12.33 billion yuan, according to the company’s stock exchange filing.
BYD blamed the revenue decline on weakness in its new energy vehicle (NEV) business, compounded by foreign-exchange losses tied to currency swings as it expands abroad.
Automotive and related products generated 275.34 billion yuan in the first half, down 8.98% and accounting for 79.85% of group revenue. The electronics division rose 0.96% to 69.41 billion yuan.
Exports are doing the heavy lifting
BYD sold 1,808,511 NEVs in the first half, down 15.72% from a year earlier. But the drop was almost entirely a domestic problem — and it narrowed sharply as the year went on.
Second-quarter sales fell just 3.24% to 1,108,048 units, a dramatic improvement from the 30.01% plunge in the first quarter.
The reason is overseas demand. BYD exported roughly 792,000 vehicles in the first half, up 67.8% year-over-year and equal to about 44% of its total sales. In the second quarter alone, overseas sales hit 471,091 units, up 82.46% and nearly 47% higher than the previous quarter.
That international push is also lifting profitability. First-half gross profit slipped 2.81% to 64.99 billion yuan, but gross margin rose to 18.85% from 18.01% a year earlier — a sign that higher-value export sales are more lucrative than the price-war volume BYD is fighting for at home.
Sales of BYD’s premium brands — Denza, Fang Cheng Bao, and Yangwang — climbed 61% and now make up 12.8% of its passenger-vehicle sales.
The China price war is the backdrop
BYD’s domestic struggles reflect the brutal price competition that has gripped China’s auto market, where Beijing has started pressuring automakers to end the “involution” of endless price cuts that have crushed margins across the industry.
BYD kept spending through the downturn. First-half R&D investment reached about 28.9 billion yuan — roughly 2.3 times its net profit for the period — bringing cumulative R&D spending above 270 billion yuan.
Operating cash flow rose 17.3% to 37.34 billion yuan, though the overseas expansion stretched BYD’s inventory turnover to 109 days from 79 a year ago, as more cars sit in transit on long ocean voyages.
Momentum heading into the second half
The recovery appears to be accelerating. July sales rose 21.76% to 419,211 units, the third consecutive month of year-over-year growth. Overseas sales of passenger vehicles and pickups hit a record 179,841 units in July, up 124.3% and about 43% of the month’s total.
BYD has told analysts it is targeting 1.5 million vehicle exports for all of 2026.
How BYD stacks up against Tesla
BYD remains the world’s largest maker of electric vehicles by volume. In the second quarter, it delivered
557,090 fully electric vehicles, well ahead of Tesla
, even before counting its plug-in hybrids.
Tesla, by comparison,
delivered 480,126 vehicles in Q2
, its own rebound quarter, but
reported record revenue alongside a big profit miss
. Both automakers are leaning on markets outside their home turf, and both are being squeezed on margins.
Electrek’s Take
Strip out the international business and this is a rough year for BYD in China. First-half deliveries fell nearly 16%, and profit is still down more than 20% for the half. The price war Beijing is now trying to cool did real damage. What saved the quarter was BYD’s ability to sell cars in Europe, Southeast Asia, and Latin America at higher margins than it can get at home — the same dynamic we’ve watched play out as
BYD outsells Tesla across Europe
and other overseas markets.
That’s a healthier revenue mix, but it comes with new risks. Inventory days jumped to 109 from 79 because cars are spending weeks on ships, tariffs in the EU and elsewhere are a moving target, and BYD is now exposed to the currency swings that already cost it real money this half. The export engine is powerful, but it’s more fragile than the domestic machine BYD built its dominance on.
Still, the trajectory is definitely better. Three straight months of sales growth, a rebuilt margin, and a 1.5-million-unit export target say BYD has found its footing again.
I think it’s fairly clear that BYD will come out on top here. Competition is fierce in China, and the automakers that will survive are those that already have a strong international presence. The dust from the price war in China will eventually settle, and BYD is likely best positioned to resume growth in the market.
Meanwhile, it’s still incredible to me that BYD brought in more profit than Tesla last quarter, and yet its market cap is roughly one-tenth of Tesla’s. Beyond the TSLA cult believing Musk, it’s hard to understand why, as I find BYD’s product roadmap way more interesting than Tesla’s. It is also catching up with advanced driver assist systems, and its battery business is a decade ahead of Tesla’s.

department of the interior

Photo by Roy Luck on
The largest benefactor of the Interior Department’s most recent
illegal wind buyout
is an Australian-American billionaire whose private equity firm will receive $900 million in exchange for a stake in a methane gas terminal in Louisiana. The near-billion-dollar buyout comes after the same billionaire gave a $1 million bribe to the originator of the deal.
At issue is the recent deal by the Department of the Interior with RWE, a German energy company that had been set to build several wind farms off the US coast.
Interior illegally gave $1.22 billion to RWE to get them to stop building these projects, and RWE will instead put $900 million of that money into purchasing a stake in a methane gas terminal in Louisiana and $300 million into building dirty methane gas turbines for data centers, which are making electricity both more expensive and dirtier.
It’s part of a pattern of wasteful spending by the Interior Department, which has so far
spent around $4 billion of taxpayer money

But it turns out the RWE deal is even more nefarious than we previously thought, as it
has now been reported

title: Qronge X1 Spark L Review: Does a $1,299 Sur-Ron Light Bee alternative cut the right corners?
content:
If you are late to the pre-teen suburban e-moto scene, we’ve been wading through the exploding market of low-cost Sur-Ron competitors over the past months. While we can all debate the safety and legality issues these bikes bring, the reality is that they are incredibly popular and useful for those who can get around their neighborhoods and back roads and are comfortable hitting speeds up to and above 40mph. Enter the low cost $1299 Qronge X1 Spark L.
Qronge has spent the last couple of years building a reputation the way most budget e-bike brands do: undercut an established category by a factor of two or three and hope the compromises don’t show up until long after the warranty window closes. The X1 Spark L is the company’s bid at the “mini electric dirt bike” segment that Sur-Ron created and Talaria, Segway, and a dozen Amazon-native brands have since piled into. However, at $1,299, it’s positioned directly against bikes that cost 3-4x as much — so the real question isn’t whether it’s fun in a parking lot. It’s whether it survives actual trail use, and whether the spec sheet is telling the truth.
For us in the last month, it has largely been a pleasant surprise.
The X1 Spark L runs the same drivetrain as the smaller X1 Spark M (and HeyBike Villan/Yozma IN 10Pro): a 4,500W peak mid-drive motor claimed to produce 283 Nm of torque, fed by a 60V 28.8Ah (1,728Wh) battery. The L steps up with 17″/14″ wheels instead of the M’s 14″/12″ setup, a full-twist throttle, and a heavier-duty 420H chain — a sensible upgrade given how much torque a budget drivetrain is being asked to absorb. Qronge claims a 50 mph top speed and up to 60 miles of range. Both of those are incredibly “optimistic,” as Electrek readers know by now, and you should expect to hit 40+mph and maaaaybe 30-mile range in real-world usage with a 200-lb rider. Qronge notes that their 60 mile claim is at just 12.5 mph and you’ll see HALF that range – 30 miles – at 22mph (!!) and just 21 miles of range at full throttle. I think this is actually being brutally honest though I don’t know if I’ve ever seen an e-Moto driver stop at 12mph.
Where it’s genuinely competitive
The torque and hill-climbing numbers aren’t just marketing. Multiple independent testers noted the same thing and I can confirm — steep, loose inclines that stall underpowered budget bikes didn’t slow this one down, and the motor itself is physically larger than the one in the Sur-Ron Light Bee X it’s obviously benchmarked against. For a bike costing roughly a third of the Sur-Ron, that’s a legitimate point in its favor, not a marketing talking point…if size is the most important factor.
The 420H heavy-duty chain is a small spec choice, but it’s the kind of thing that tells you whether an engineering team is thinking past launch day. A 4,500W motor putting torque through a standard 420 chain is a wear-item failure waiting to happen; Qronge apparently anticipated that point of failure.
Corners were cut to get to $1299
The 2A charger is the typical corner-cutting move, saving $50 or so over a quicker 4-6A option. We’ll allow it on this e-moto because you can always upgrade it yourself or maybe 30 miles/day is plenty for your riding needs. But expect longer charge times on the Qronge than the top shelf e-motos.
The seat is not comfortable, and I’d taken to putting a towel under my keister for longer rides. For people like my teen without back issues, it wasn’t even a consideration so your mileage will vary here.
Fit and finish are par for a $1299 e-moto. It took a hammer to get one of the pegs in. Some of the screws didn’t feel threaded properly, and parts like the rear shock took a while to assemble. However, the bike eventually came together nicely and those extra minutes of assembly are just a forgotten memory now.
The biggest problem, and one I think deserves a significant pause, is that the brake levers here are very cost-cutter. The bottom line is that they do work fine but the limited travel and ability to use one finger are severely limited. We didn’t have any outages and the hydraulics worked fine for the month of testing, but this is one corner I don’t like to cut.

Electrek’s take:
The Qronge X1 Spark L looks like a legitimate budget alternative to the Sur-Ron-style mini dirt bike category — if you go in accepting that “budget” means some inconsistent components, limited brakes and a seat you’ll probably replace if you are an adult, and if you mentally discount the range claim by roughly a half before you ever throw a leg over it.
Strangely, after all was said and done, this bike actually performed quite well and is still one of the our favorites in the budget stable. The bigger 14/17 wheels take it above the Tuttio/Yozma/Heybike 14/12 class where it is priced at so if the budget doesn’t reach close to $2000, I say go for it. It is also a fairly good-looking bike, and I can recommend it as long as the caveats above aren’t dealbreakers.

title: Ontario airport set to spend $5.5 million on electric ground support equipment
content:
Commercial EVs
aviation
Jo Borrás
| Aug 28 2026 - 4:41 am PT
California’s Ontario International Airport (ONT) has been awarded a $~4.15 million grant from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to expand its zero emission infrastructure and add more electric ground support equipment (GSE).
With the short distances driven at limited speeds under extreme loads
, ground handling and support equipment (GHE/GSE) at airports present a nearly ideal use case for battery-electric vehicles. That’s a good thing, too.
As demand for on-road fossil fuels drops
, airports and airlines –
historically responsible for about 4% Earth’s global warming
– are becoming a bigger and bigger slice of a rapidly shrinking pie when it comes to the fossil fuel emissions generated by the aviation and air travel industries as a whole,
making investment in this sector extra impactful
“This latest investment by the FAA is a tremendous vote of confidence in the work we are doing to build a more sustainable Ontario International Airport,” explains Atif Elkadi, chief executive officer of the Ontario International Airport Authority. “Three VALE grants in three years represents meaningful progress, and this latest award will allow us and our airline partners to continue reducing emissions while investing in the infrastructure ONT will need for the future.”
The Federal Voluntary Airport Low Emissions (VALE) grant program helps airports meet air-quality goals by funding eligible projects that reduce GHG emissions. ONT’s latest award will reduce the need for aircraft and ground equipment to burn fuel while parked at the terminal, supporting cleaner and more efficient airport operations – and, after Ontario’s 25% cost match, the $4,147,752 will bring total spending on electric GSE at Terminals 2 and 4 to $5.53 million.

Autonomous baggage handler; via OshKosh.

title: Investments in co-located solar-plus-storage reach $25 billion in H1, says BloombergNEF - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Global renewable energy investment reached $327.5 billion in the first half of 2026, as capital shifted toward solar-plus-storage projects amid growing revenue uncertainty. US investment surged ahead of tax credit deadlines, while weaker activity in China and offshore wind weighed on the global outlook.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
28 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
A solar-plus-storage facility in Chile
Global investment in renewable energy reached $327.5 billion (€281 billion) in the first half of 2026, virtually unchanged from the previous six months but 21% below the record set in the second half of 2024.
Data from BloombergNEF (BNEF) show that renewable energy deployment remains on track despite regulatory changes in key markets, including the United States and China. Investment, however, is increasingly shifting toward assets that offer greater flexibility in managing revenues.
Storage drives hybrid projects
Financing for standalone utility-scale solar fell more sharply than investment in onshore wind. Investment in standalone solar PV declined 20% year on year to $75.4 billion (€64.7 billion), its lowest level since the solar investment boom began in 2021.
Growing revenue uncertainty, driven by solar price cannibalization, curtailment and grid congestion, is pushing investors and developers toward more flexible project configurations.
Against this backdrop, co-located solar-plus-storage projects attracted a record $25 billion (€21.5 billion) in investment in the first half of 2026. The figure was nearly double the total recorded in the second half of 2025 and three times the amount invested in the first half of that year. The United States and Australia led investment in the segment.
US accelerates ahead of incentive expiration
The United States was the second-largest market for renewable energy investment, behind China but ahead of the European Union, recording 54% year-on-year growth. Developers accelerated project financing to meet tax credit deadlines and respond to surging electricity demand, driven in part by data centers.
Solar investment rose 41% to a record $45.8 billion (€39.3 billion), while wind investment reached $13.8 billion, more than double the previous year’s figure. Projects that remain eligible for tax credits could sustain construction activity in the short term, with the final installations scheduled through 2030.
European onshore wind holds firm
Global wind investment totaled $92.3 billion, down 27% year on year. Offshore wind was particularly hard hit, with investment plunging 72% amid poor auction results, higher capital and financing costs and a shrinking pipeline of projects likely to reach financial close.
Onshore wind investment declined by a more moderate 4% to $80.7 billion. Europe, however, bucked the trend, with Germany, Romania and Serbia all recording record investment levels following recent auctions.
China accounted for just one-quarter of global investment, down from more than half in 2022, following reforms to its electricity market. By contrast, Vietnam quadrupled its investment, while investment across Southeast Asia surpassed $12 billion. Nigeria increased investment in distributed solar and storage, Central Asia maintained investment above $4 billion, and Brazil helped push global biofuel investment to $7.7 billion.
BloombergNEF expects new renewable energy installations in 2026 to fall below 2025 levels, marking the first year-on-year decline in more than a decade. It expects growth to resume in 2027.

title: The Hydrogen Stream: Africa’s first PV-driven hydrogen hub powers up - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Cbm-Tech has launched a green hydrogen hub in Walvis Bay combining 5 MW of solar, a 5 MW PEM electrolyzer and 5.9 MWh of battery storage.
Sergio Matalucci
28 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Energy Storage
Highlights
Hydrogen
Namibia’s first green hydrogen production plant – the Hydrogen Dune – also incorporates a refuelling station and hydrogen academy.
Cmb-Tech
has started operations at a green hydrogen facility in Walvis Bay featuring 5 MW of off-grid solar, a 5 MW proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzer and 5.9 MWh of battery energy storage. The project, developed with Namibia’s Ohlthaver & List Group, has around 7,000 solar modules installed across 6.5 hectares. The developers describe it as Africa’s first fully integrated green hydrogen facility. Hydrogen produced at the site will be used in dual-fuel trucks and generators, with railway and maritime applications also planned. CMB.TECH is an initial offtaker and plans to test a hydrogen-powered freight locomotive. Siemens supplied the facility’s integrated electrical, automation and safety systems. The site also includes a hydrogen refueling station and a training center. Cmb.Tech said it plans to scale the project first to 250 MW and later to 500 MW, with potential future production of green ammonia for maritime applications. The facility adds to Namibia’s emerging hydrogen sector. HyIron’s Oshivela project began producing green hydrogen in March 2025 using a 12 MW electrolyzer powered by a 25 MW solar plant.
Tohoku University
researchers have used iron oxide in a photocatalytic reaction to split water using light energy. The Japanese researchers found that photocatalytic water splitting occurs when iron oxide doped with about 1% titanium is combined with rhodium-doped strontium titanate, a hydrogen-generating photocatalyst. Electrochemical measurements showed that titanium doping reduces electrical resistance and improves n-type semiconductor properties, promoting the separation of photogenerated electrons and holes and enabling water-splitting activity.
Researchers at the
University of Nottingham
have investigated the microscopic structure of metal swarf from manufacturing processes as a potential substrate for hydrogen-production catalysts. Using advanced imaging, the UK researchers found nanoscale grooves and ridges on waste stainless steel, titanium and nickel alloys that can act as anchoring sites for precious metals. The team deposited small amounts of platinum onto the waste metal to produce electrocatalysts capable of splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen.
Researchers at
Durham University
have found that suitable depleted North Sea fields could provide
3,659 TWh
of hydrogen storage capacity, equivalent to more than seven years of projected UK electricity demand in 2040. The researchers said using the fields for hydrogen storage could also enable conventional gas-fired power plants to be phased out of the UK electricity system by 2040. Current UK hydrogen storage plans focus on salt caverns and do not include depleted fields.
Researchers at
Seoul National University of Science and Technology
(Seoultech) have developed an AI-based system that increased the hydrogen production efficiency of a solid oxide electrolysis cell system by 14% while reducing internal temperature spikes by 80%. The researchers said the approach uses machine learning to identify the most informative simulations, reducing the computational resources required to determine promising operating conditions while limiting thermal stresses that can affect equipment lifetime.

The policy calls for hydrogen and its derivatives to be integrated with the country’s existing oil and gas infrastructure, including its extensive pipeline network. The plan does not specify quantitative targets, with implementation expected to depend on hydrogen market development and cooperation with local governments.

title: Wood Mackenzie raises Latin America storage forecast to 34 GW by 2035 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Wood Mackenzie forecasts Latin America’s energy storage capacity to surge from 2.5 GW in 2025 to 34 GW by 2035, driven by renewable curtailment, grid constraints, auctions, and supportive policies. Chile leads deployment, while Mexico, Brazil, Argentina, and the Dominican Republic are scaling up, though unclear revenue models, financing constraints, and regulatory gaps remain key barriers.
Luis Ini
28 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Americas
Batteries
Energy Storage
Highlights
Utility-scale
A storage facility operated by Grenergy in Latin America
Wood Mackenzie expects energy storage deployment in Latin America to accelerate sharply over the next decade. In its new “Latin America Energy Storage Outlook 2026” report, the consultancy forecasts cumulative capacity to increase from 2.5 GW in 2025 to 34 GW in 2035, representing a 13.6-fold increase in installed capacity over 10 years.
The new forecast represents a substantial revision from the previous edition of the report. In September 2025, Wood Mackenzie projected that the Latin American market would reach 23 GW in 2034, with a compound annual growth rate of 8%. At the time, it had already identified grid constraints, rising renewable energy curtailment, and auctions as the main drivers of energy storage deployment.
“Latin America is no longer a frontier market for energy storage, it is an active market. The project pipeline is growing rapidly, but deployment stalls without comprehensive regulatory frameworks with clear remuneration mechanisms,” said Pamela Morales of Wood Mackenzie.
Chile remains the regional leader and has the largest battery energy storage system (BESS) projects currently in operation in Latin America. According to the consultancy, high levels of renewable energy curtailment continue to support investment in longer-duration systems. However, Wood Mackenzie identifies a new risk: price cannibalization in northern Chile as battery capacity increases, which could reduce revenues from energy arbitrage.
Mexico is at an inflection point driven largely by energy policy, according to the analysis. Wood Mackenzie estimates that new mechanisms for strategic projects and joint development schemes with Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE), which include storage, could result in more than 3 GW of capacity being awarded through 2030.
Mexico’s call for strategic projects established an indicative target in July of 935 MW of standalone energy storage systems, all with three-hour durations, across Baja California, Baja California Sur, and the North, Northwest, Eastern, Western, and Peninsular regions. The figure is indicative and does not constitute a limit on project submissions. In addition, the Electricity Sector Development Plan includes a storage requirement equivalent to 30% of the capacity of new renewable energy projects, according to Wood Mackenzie’s analysis.
Brazil is also preparing for a change in scale. The country will hold its first two capacity reserve auctions specifically for large-scale battery systems on Dec. 2 and Dec. 4, 2026. The first will be reserved for projects that meet domestic manufacturing requirements, while the second will be open to other systems. Contracts will run for 15 years, with supply beginning Aug. 1, 2028, and facilities will be required to have at least 30 MW of power capacity and four hours of duration.
Wood Mackenzie expects these auctions to accelerate additions in Brazil from 2028, although it warns that financing will remain constrained while sufficiently clear and predictable remuneration mechanisms are absent.
Argentina, meanwhile, has established a standalone energy storage market supported by auctions in little more than a year. The Wood Mackenzie report puts recent awards at around 1.3 GW, while available official data totals 1,413.5 MW. AlmaGBA awarded 713 MW, while AlmaSADI awarded a further 700.5 MW. The projects are primarily intended to ease constraints at critical grid nodes and provide power and reserve services while transmission network upgrades are carried out.
The Dominican Republic is identified in the report as one of the Caribbean markets with a more developed regulatory framework. Regulations require new renewable energy projects of at least 20 MWac to include storage equivalent to at least 50% of their installed capacity, with a minimum duration of four hours. Wood Mackenzie also puts the country’s storage target at 500 MW by 2030.
Despite the expected growth, the consultancy identifies the lack of bankable revenue models as the region’s main obstacle. In many markets, remuneration for ancillary services, energy arbitrage, or capacity has yet to be defined, while financing constraints, permitting delays, and a limited number of buyers able to support long-term contracts add further challenges.
Morales said Latin America needs to strike a balance between mandates and incentives to support market development. She added that countries with bankable remuneration mechanisms will be better placed to convert announced project pipelines into operational assets over the next decade.

title: Canada’s solar sector sees growing momentum across differing provincial markets - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
While Canada’s provinces and territories continue to prioritise solar to different degrees, US tariff uncertainty is reinforcing national-level plans to invest in renewables and more integrated energy infrastructure.
Patrick Jowett
28 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Americas
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Utility-scale
Solar development is accelerating in some parts of Canada, while others are taking a more cautious approach as provinces and territories chart their own energy policies.
Phil McKay, Senior Director of Member Programs at the Canadian Renewable Energy Association (CanREA), told
pv magazine
that while figures for new solar additions in 2026 are not yet available, he is hearing anecdotally from the association’s members that it has been “a good year”, with many talking about growing interest in storage-paired systems.
Canada’s solar market is highly fragmented across its ten provinces and three territories. This is largely down to the country’s electricity system, which the federal government’s website describes as multiple, relatively-segregated grids that are governed and planned independently and generally trade more with the US than one another. McKay described it as “13 different markets.”
These markets are prioritizing solar buildout to different degrees. In April, Québec launched a solar incentive program, with provincial utility Hydro-Québec offering a direct cash rebate of CAN 1,000 ($720)/kW covering up to 40% of eligible installation costs for residential and customer customers.
According to details on its website, the support cuts the current payback period of 25-30 years down to 10-12 years. It forms part of wider plans to integrate
3 GW of solar
in Québec by 2035. “Speaking with local companies there, they’ve been ran off their feet with inquiries [since the launch],” McKay said.
Another solar market leader is Ontario, which
backed 12 solar projects with a combined capacity of 915 MW
through its long-term energy procurement exercise in April. Such procurements are a key driver of Canada’s solar market, with previous CanREA analysis expecting them to be a large contributor to a forecasted
21 GW of solar by 2035
The awarded projects in Ontario are granted 20-year agreements and are expected to begin commercial operation by the start of May 2030. McKay added that the approvals include agrivoltaics projects. “This is an open cost-competitive environment where agrivoltaics are competing with gas, which is so great to see,” he said.
Other regions of the country are starting to entertain a shift from net-metering to net-billing. British Columbia has replaced net metering with a fixed CAN 0.10/kWh export rate below retail, while New Brunswick is proposing a similar shift to below-retail compensation for surplus solar generation.
“Its all based on the same premise that solar isn’t as valuable as we’ve been making it out to be and solar customers are getting a free ride,” McKay explained. “There is huge pushback in the province, a lot of people are very upset about it.”
McKay spoke with
pv magazine
soon after the US placed 50% tariffs on many billions of dollars worth of Canadian goods going into the States last weekend. He said the uncertainty around US policy decisions impacts the entire sector.
“Everything [the US administration] does affects us, even content requirements on Chinese imports can create pathways for us. It’s hard to forecast where this goes because two weeks ago, we didn’t know we’d face these tariffs,” he said.
Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to the latest tariffs with a speech that McKay said reiterated commitments from the spring budget to double the electricity grid with sustainable energy.
“That’s very policy-driven language for solar, wind, and storage markets,” McKay said. He added that the ‘build Canada strong’ narrative is helping to unify the country around energy infrastructure.
“We’re finally talking about cross-Canada transmission lines and nation-building projects,” he said. “That’s exciting because it’ll open up the solar market and help balance the grid.”
On the other end of the scale, McKay shared that Canada’s grassroots solar movement is also picking up. Discussions around plug-in solar are developing, with the Canadian Standards Association currently debating UL 3700, a bi-national safety framework for Canada and the US that covers interactive plug-in solar systems.
McKay explained that while the standards ecosystem is engaged, progress is expected to move slowly. In the meantime, community and environmental organisations are starting to show interest in such products. “They see these systems as energy freedom,” McKay said. “A way to give Canadians a choice over whether we burn fossil fuels or not.”
McKay added that some large authorities, such as Ontario’s Electrical Safety Authority, are saying they will back UL 3700-compliant products, but he also confirmed that no such products are yet available.
“A few manufacturers are starting to design products to that standard,” McKay said. “It’s nascent, [now] waiting for the next steps before getting the standards, then we can unlock the whole country.”

title: Europe’s solar resource surplus continues before late-August cloud shift - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
In a new weekly update for
pv magazine
, Solcast, a DNV company, reports that Europe’s solar irradiance averaged 5% above the 2007–2025 norm in August 2026, with nearly three-quarters of the continent seeing above-average levels due to persistent high pressure and clear skies. Conditions shifted later in the month as cooler, cloudier weather reduced gains in western Europe, while central and eastern regions retained much of their irradiance surplus.
28 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Utility-scale
Global horizontal irradiance across Europe averaged 5% above the 2007–2025 norm in August 2026, extending the elevated solar resource recorded during June and July, according to analysis using the
Solcast API
. Nearly three quarters of the continent received above-average irradiance as persistent high pressure limited cloud formation and storm development. Much of southern England experienced Europe’s strongest positive anomalies, reaching more than 20% above average, before a change in weather patterns brought cooler and cloudier conditions to parts of western Europe during the second half of the month.
High pressure remained the main influence on Europe’s solar resource for much of August. Sinking air within the persistent system stabilised atmospheric conditions, limiting cloud formation and supporting extended periods of clear sky. Although August is typically Europe’s second-sunniest month, irradiance reached more than 20% above the seasonal norm in some regions. This marked a third consecutive month of elevated solar resource across much of western and central Europe, while London’s cumulative GHI reached a record high for this point in the year.
The unusually sunny conditions coincided with exceptional drought across parts of Europe. Southern England experienced 62 consecutive dry days through the middle of August, easily breaking the previous record of 51 days. According to the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre, critically low levels on the Rhine and Danube disrupted hydropower and nuclear generation, increasing reliance on other generation sources, including solar.
In Birmingham, the prolonged lack of rainfall provided few opportunities for natural module cleaning, allowing modelled soiling losses to accumulate before rain returned in mid-August.
The prolonged high-pressure pattern began to break down during the second half of August. As the system weakened and shifted eastward, a cold front arrived from the Atlantic and temperatures fell by more than 15 C across parts of western Europe after weeks of persistent heat and dry weather. Increasing cloud and rainfall reduced the earlier irradiance surplus as the front moved into France and Germany.
The late-month change had an uneven effect on Europe’s irradiance. Central and eastern regions retained more of their earlier surplus, while parts of southwestern Europe finished closer to or below their long-term average.
Porto’s daily irradiance profiles provide a closer view of the changing conditions in the southwest. Early-month profiles were generally more consistent, while several days around and after mid-month recorded pronounced daytime reductions.

title: Machine learning improves irradiance prediction in bifacial PV systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
A Selçuk University researcher has compared six machine learning algorithms for predicting front- and rear-side plane-of-array irradiance in bifacial PV systems. Random forest delivered the best results for both sides, while rear-side irradiance proved more difficult to predict.
Lior Kahana
28 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Enerray solar PV plant in Turkey
A researcher at Turkey’s
Selçuk University
has conducted a comparative analysis of multiple machine learning algorithms for predicting plane-of-array (PoA) irradiance on bifacial PV panels. The researcher used identical input conditions to predict PoA irradiance on both the front and rear sides of the panels.
“This study presented a comprehensive machine learning–based framework for predicting front-side and rear-side PoA irradiance in a bifacial photovoltaic system using routinely measured meteorological, surface-related, and temporal input variables,” researcher Ayşegül Toprak said in the paper. “This study demonstrates that accurate and interpretable prediction of both front and rear PoA irradiance can be achieved using a compact set of easily measurable inputs.”
The study used synchronized field measurements collected between Nov. 17, 2023, and May 29, 2024, from a vertical bifacial PV testbed operated by the US Department of Energy’s National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) in Golden, Colorado. The testbed consisted of a vertically mounted bifacial PV array positioned close to the ground, along with meteorological sensors, ground-reflected irradiance measurements and six IMT reference cells.
The input dataset included global horizontal irradiance (GHI), diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI), ambient temperature, wind speed, testbed albedo and a binary reflector variable, as well as hour_sin and hour_cos, which represent the daily solar cycle. Before model training, the researcher removed physically implausible zero values, sensor faults and records containing missing or inconsistent measurements.
Toprak then evaluated six regression algorithms: linear regression, k-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector regression (SVR) with a radial basis function kernel, random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) and a feedforward multilayer perceptron (MLP). Each model was run separately for front and rear PoA irradiance using the same input variables and identical five-fold cross-validation partitions in MATLAB. Predictive accuracy was assessed using root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE) and the Pearson correlation coefficient (r).
The results showed that nonlinear models clearly outperformed linear regression in predicting both front- and rear-side irradiance. Random forest achieved the best performance for front PoA irradiance, with an RMSE of 0.188, an MAE of 0.061 and a correlation coefficient of 0.982. It was followed closely by MLP, XGBoost and SVR, all of which recorded correlation coefficients above 0.97.
Rear PoA irradiance proved more difficult to predict. Random forest again performed best, with an RMSE of 0.236, an MAE of 0.080 and an r value of 0.973, while MLP recorded the same RMSE but a slightly higher MAE of 0.086. Linear regression ranked last for both targets, with RMSE values of 0.682 for front PoA irradiance and 0.593 for rear PoA irradiance.
“The results indicate that front-side irradiance is primarily governed by global irradiance and diurnal solar geometry, whereas rear-side irradiance is strongly influenced by surface-related factors such as ground albedo and the presence of reflective ground cover, confirming the conditional and interaction-driven nature of rear-side irradiance formation in bifacial systems,” Toprak concluded.
The study, “
Front and rear plane-of-array irradiance in bifacial photovoltaic systems: A machine learning-based prediction approach
,” was published in
Energy Reports
