title: Data Center Backlash Reaches the Ballot Box
content:
At least 18 incumbent officeholders lost elections between August 2025 and August 2026 after taking documented action on a data center project or becoming associated with a political fight over its development, according to a
Data Center Knowledge
review of election results, government records, campaign materials, and local reporting.
The cases are not equally conclusive. In some, defeated officials directly attributed their losses to data center votes. In others, challengers made data centers a prominent campaign issue alongside electricity costs, taxes, land use or local control.
Data Center Knowledge
counted an incumbent officeholder only when the official lost a completed election after a documented vote, approval, incentive, zoning action or public advocacy connected to a data center project or policy controversy. The review does not treat timing alone as proof that the issue determined the result.
Related:
Land Banking Explained: A Novel Strategy for Data Center Expansion
The count includes one officeholder, Bridget McCandless in Missouri, who sought the mayor’s office while serving as an incumbent council member. It is a count of documented losses, not a measurement of how often data center involvement causes an incumbent to lose.
The officials themselves have generally been reluctant to publicly attribute their defeats to data centers. Their opponents have been considerably less reluctant to make the connection.
Utah produced the clearest examples. State Senate President J. Stuart Adams
lost his Republican primary in June
to Stephanie Hollist after becoming closely associated with the proposed Stratos data center project in Box Elder County.
Two Box Elder County commissioners, Lee Perry and Boyd Bingham, also
lost their Republican primaries
after voting to advance the project.
The proposed Stratos project has drawn opposition over potential water and environmental impacts. The
commissioners voted
to allow the state’s Military Installation Development Authority to
create the Stratos project area
, giving the state authority to override county zoning and land-use regulations.
Hollist made opposition to Stratos a central campaign issue.
Perry was unusually direct about the political consequences after his defeat.
“Do I think that the data center vote cost me the election? Yes I do,” Perry told
The Salt Lake Tribune
after conceding his primary race.
Adams, who chairs the MIDA board
, also faced pressure over the project and moved late in the campaign to soften his position on its proposed footprint.
The Utah cases provide the clearest evidence in the review that data center politics can reach beyond local zoning fights and threaten senior state officials.
Related:
Praetorian’s Virginia Megasite Could Accommodate Data Center Development
Missouri
Missouri produced another cluster – and one of the most revealing cases. In Festus,
four incumbent city council members
– Jimmy Collier, Brian Wehner, Bobby Venz, and Jim Tinnin – lost their elections after a fight over a
proposed $6 billion data center project
Collier, Venz, and Tinnin voted for the development agreement, while Wehner voted against it. All four lost.
That makes it difficult to characterize the backlash as nothing more than punishment for voting yes. The controversy also involved the city’s development process, transparency and the way the agreement was approved.
In Independence, council members Jared Fears and Bridget McCandless also lost elections amid a fight over a proposed data center and associated tax incentives.
Fears later said the project was a factor in his defeat.
The Missouri cases show that the political exposure can come from the project itself, the approval process or an official’s association with a broader development fight.
Campaign Attacks
The pattern extends beyond Missouri and Utah. In North Carolina, David Batts defeated four-term Edgecombe County Commissioner Donald Boswell after campaigning explicitly against the proposed Kingsboro data center. Batts had warned commissioners that residents would “primary” them over the project.
Related:
AWS Data Center Withdrawal Signals Growing Political, Community Challenges
His campaign signs said: “Vote no for data centers.”
In Virginia, meanwhile, Democrat John McAuliff branded Republican Del. Geary Higgins “Data Center Geary” and made data centers a major attack line in his successful challenge.
Maryland offered a different version of the backlash: officials who had opposed a pause on new data center development still became targets of candidates who argued the county had mishandled growth.
Calvert County commissioners Todd Ireland, Mark Cox Sr. and Earl “Buddy” Hance lost their Republican primaries after challengers criticized their opposition to
a proposed pause
on new data center development and the county’s broader handling of growth.
Frederick County Council President Brad Young also lost his Democratic primary after the council approved a
zoning expansion
that opened more than 2,600 acres to data center development.
Oregon state Sen. Janeen Sollman lost her Democratic primary in a race that included opposition to data center development in the Hillsboro area. Labor and education issues also played major roles, making the data center connection less direct.
Georgia Public Service Commissioner Tim Echols lost his reelection bid in a race dominated by electricity rates and Georgia Power. Data centers were part of the broader debate over who should pay for new generation and grid infrastructure, but the evidence connecting the issue directly to his defeat is weaker.
The cases differ in their evidentiary strength. But together they show a change in political incentives: candidates now see data centers as shorthand for broader complaints about power costs, tax policy, land use and local control.
Industry Response
Mike Casey, president of Tigercomm, an energy tech PR firm, said the industry has underestimated the need to campaign for projects.
“Most tech companies weren’t built to campaign for what they need to build,” Casey told
Data Center Knowledge
. “But winning a community’s permission to build in its midst is the opposite. It’s one county at a time, it’s heavily retail, and it’s person-driven.”
Casey said developers accustomed to rapid permitting are now operating in a “high-friction permitting environment” and are trying to build community-engagement operations after encountering widespread opposition.
“Too many developers are trying to bulldoze projects through instead of skillfully campaigning for them,” he said.
The result, he said, is “a community relations problem metastasizing into a widespread political crisis.”
The Data Center Coalition’s response has focused more on explaining the industry’s economic contribution.
Dan Diorio, the coalition’s executive vice president of state policy and government affairs, said in an email to
Data Center Knowledge
that the industry understands the need for “continued efforts to better explain the role of data centers to the public through community engagement and stakeholder education.”
Diorio cited a PwC report estimating that the industry supported 5.5 million jobs, contributed $927 billion to US GDP, and generated $204 billion in federal, state and local taxes in 2024.
He also said data centers are committed to paying for the energy they consume and being responsible partners in the communities where they operate.
Jeff Thramann, founder and CEO of LT350, a company developing distributed data center infrastructure, argues that communication alone will not resolve the backlash.
“I think fundamental change is required because the impact of huge data centers on a single community is real,” Thramann said.
His prescription is to distribute computing capacity across smaller facilities rather than concentrate hundreds of megawatts at individual sites.
“If 300 MWs of capacity is needed in one location, the impact on that geography compared to spreading 1 MW across 300 grid circuits is incredibly different,” he said.
Thramann said the public distinguishes between a massive centralized campus and smaller computing facilities that have little visible effect on a community.
“A data center can range from an enormous, centralized facility to a closet in an office,” he said. “The public does not care about the closet because it changes nothing in a community, but they do care about the giant facility that changes an entire community.”
State Policy
Data centers are also appearing in paid campaign advertising well beyond the local governments that approve projects.
Campaigns in Ohio, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Texas and Michigan have attacked candidates or elected officials over data center development, electricity costs, tax incentives or ties to developers.
Those races are separate from the 18 completed losses. They show that campaigns increasingly view data centers as a viable attack vector, but they do not establish an electoral penalty.
State leaders are also adjusting policy as concerns about power costs, permitting, incentives, and local opposition intensify.
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, once a strong promoter of data center investment, is pushing to slow new projects and prevent their costs from being shifted to other customers. He said in August that data center companies had “basically dug their own grave” by failing to win community support.
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has added environmental and transparency requirements for data center development, while Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has paused new data center tax-exemption requests.
The moves do not necessarily amount to opposition to data center development. They impose different conditions on its expansion – around electricity, water, permitting, transparency and incentives.
The Political Cost
The 18 races do not prove that data centers caused 18 defeats. They show that data center development has become a political vulnerability that candidates can exploit.
In the strongest cases, officials took documented actions on projects, challengers made those actions campaign issues, and the incumbents lost. In weaker cases, data centers became one issue in broader fights over electricity, taxes, development and local control.
The political bargain around data centers is changing. Developers still offer investment, jobs, and tax revenue, but communities are increasingly asking who pays for the electricity, who bears the effects on water and land, whether tax incentives are justified and how much say residents have before a project is approved.
Those questions are now following data center projects into elections.
And once an opponent can turn a permitting fight into a campaign issue, the project has acquired a political cost that can outlast the public hearing.

title: AI Rack Density’s Real Limits: Power, Cooling, Failure Risk
content:
For decades, each new generation of hardware has packed more compute into less space. AI accelerated that trend to a pace data centers have never seen before, as operators try to squeeze maximum performance from every rack in AI factory deployments.
The change has been dramatic. Racks that seemed extreme two years ago now look ordinary, with the next jump already on the build sheet. The numbers tell the story. One common benchmark is “modal rack density,” the most frequently reported power draw per rack. In 2026, that figure reached 11 kW, up from 9 kW in 2025, according to Uptime Institute’s 16
Annual Global Data Center Survey. The 11 kW profile describes a typical enterprise server room – the kind you’d actually walk past in most data centers today – not an AI training cluster.
AI racks live in a different power class entirely. Nvidia’s GB300 NVL72 – central to AI training clusters through 2025 and early 2026 – requires up to 142 kW per rack, according to Nvidia’s NVL72 AI Factory
reference architecture
. Nvidia’s newest platform, Vera Rubin NVL72,
entered full production
in June 2026 and is slated to ship to cloud providers this fall. While Nvidia hasn’t published an official rack power figure, trade-press supply chain reports place it between
190 kW and 230 kW
. Behind it, Nvidia’s Rubin Ultra NVL576 “Kyber” rack is already specified at
roughly 600 kW
in the second half of 2027.
Related:
AI Infrastructure Pushes Data Center Capex Forecast Above $3 Trillion
So, what really caps density? Three questions define the ceiling: how much heat a rack can remove, how much power the chips draw, and how much power the facility can safely deliver.
The problem isn’t chip count, and it isn’t something bigger fans can fix. “The biggest misconception about what’s limiting density is that it’s capped by the number of GPUs per chassis, or that it’s a cooling issue that you solve with bigger fans,” Joseph Wolff, founder and CTO of eRacks Systems, told
Data Center Knowledge.
Air Cooling Has Reached Its Limit, and Liquid Has Taken Over
More compute means more heat, and for years, heat removal has set the hard limit on density. That limit keeps shifting as cooling technology improves.
Air Cooling Becomes Impractical
Air cooling becomes impractical above roughly 50 kW per rack, according to
Uptime Institute
. Past that point, fans just can’t move enough air to keep up with the thermal load.
Direct-to-Chip Is Now Standard
Liquid delivered through cold plates on the chip now handles 100 to 150 kW per rack and has become the dominant liquid method, holding
55% market share
as of 2026, according to Schneider Electric.
Related:
AI Drives Data Center Uncertainty in Uptime’s 2026 Survey
Two-Phase Immersion Is Recovering, Not Dead
Once touted as the endgame, two-phase immersion was knocked back when PFAS restrictions choked off coolant supply. Adoption hasn’t fully recovered. A replacement fluid was
qualified in early 2026
, though the regulatory outcome won’t be resolved until 2027. “Microfluidics is the one I would still call ‘roadmap talk.’ The science is proven, but mainstream deployment is still a few years off,” said Omkar Nimbalkar, vice president, multi-vendor support services, at IBM, in an interview with
Data Center Knowledge
The Next Step Is Inside the Chip
In September 2025, Microsoft and Swiss startup Corintis
reported lab tests
showing that microchannels etched directly into a chip can remove heat up to three times more effectively than a standard cold plate.
Power Delivery, Not Cooling, Sets the Real Ceiling
Thermal physics isn’t the only constraint. Power delivery is proving just as binding, and it’s not the chip specifications that ultimately decide the limit.
“People benchmark density against chip specs when, in practice, it’s bounded by electrical engineering and failure planning,” Nimbalkar said.
Legacy 54 VDC Hits the Copper Wall
Legacy 54 VDC power distribution runs into a hard limit above
roughly 200 kW per rack
, when the copper required to carry that current becomes too thick, heavy, and unwieldy to build.

Redundancy Imposes a Capacity Tax
A typical power distribution unit (PDU) handles about 20 kW, with a double-redundant configuration, while servers draw up to 6 kW each, Nimbalkar noted. “The design question is never how many GPUs you can buy, but how many you can safely run if a power supply fails,” he said.
The Power Feed, Not the Chip, Ultimately Sets the Limit
Chip vendors already design around these constraints, offering the same GPU at different power levels to fit within practical envelopes. “The real limit is the power and thermal budget per box, and it’s set by the GPUs themselves,” Wolff said. “Nvidia sells the same 96GB RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell as a 600 W part and as a 300 W Max-Q part – that second SKU exists because eight 600 W cards in one 4U is a 5 kW-class thermal problem most air-cooled rooms can’t feed or exhaust.”
Fixes Are Already Moving from Pilot to Standard
Several efforts are underway to narrow the gap between what a rack demands and what a facility can deliver.
Higher-Voltage DC Distribution Is Moving Beyond Pilots
Vera Rubin NVL72 already
ships with 800 VDC
. The transition has moved beyond pilots: Vertiv, Schneider Electric, Eaton, and Delta all have
commercial 800 VDC offerings slated
for the second half of 2026, and
Foxconn’s 40 MW Kaohsiung-1 facility
in Taiwan is being built for it. But hardware availability isn’t the same as widespread adoption. “Ultimately, we’re asking organizations to digest a generation’s worth of change in 18-24 months,” Chris Butler, president of embedded and critical power at Flex, told
Data Center Knowledge
Power Delivery Is Being Disaggregated from Compute Racks
The Open Compute Project’s Mount Diablo project reached a
finalized 0.7.0 specification
in March 2026; Microsoft and Meta demonstrated
working hardware built on it
in July 2026. By separating power delivery from compute, facilities can scale power independently of the racks it feeds.
On-Site and Behind-the-Meter Generation Are Gaining Traction
More operators are building their own power capacity rather than waiting on utility timelines. Campus-level power “on paper” doesn’t guarantee you can deliver it reliably to a single rack.
“Once you start operating at those densities, power distribution and cooling really have to move together, so the number I pay more attention to isn’t necessarily how many megawatts a campus has on paper,” said Christopher Miglino, CEO of Axe Compute, in an interview with
Data Center Knowledge
. “It’s how much of that power you can actually deliver, cool, and operate reliably.”
Where the Ceiling Will Likely Sit Three to Five Years Out
Heat removal, power delivery, failure risk, and cost each carry an open question over the next three to five years. Where those four land together will shape what “typical” looks like.
The Grid, Not the Rack, Will Be Decisive
Power availability will be decisive. As of the end of 2025, more than 2,060 GW of generation and storage were waiting in US interconnection queues, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s
Queued Up report
“On-site generation is a little more dependent on the project, but it’s becoming a much more serious part of the conversation for mega-scale AI campuses because, in many markets, the constraint isn’t demand or access to GPUs – it’s how quickly you can actually get enough power from the grid,” Miglino said.
As Racks Become Denser, Failures Become Costlier
As density climbs, a
single failure
knocks out more compute than it used to. That raises the bar for detection and graceful degradation.
“The smarter approach is building in firmware-level failure detection that can throttle a rack down in seconds, which allows you to run denser than a conservative static number would normally allow,” Nimbalkar said.
The most likely default is 100 kW or more per rack. “A typical high-density AI rack in 2028 is probably a 100 kW-plus deployment with direct liquid cooling standard, 400 V power delivery, and failure-handling logic built into the firmware rather than added as an afterthought,” Nimbalkar said.
Miglino expects the same threshold, with the leading edge well beyond it.
Wolff, however, expects a bifurcation: most enterprises will stay air-cooled, while a smaller set of headline racks will charge far past 100 kW. “The typical high-density AI rack – what most enterprises will actually deploy – is air-cooled 4U nodes with eight GPUs each at 300 W-class power, about 4 kW per box, three or four boxes per rack on ordinary 208 V feeds,” Wolff said.
